name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT8_Q01 - IUPAC definition of transition elements

questiontext.text: According to the IUPAC definition, which group of \(d\)-block elements is NOT regarded as transition metals because its members have a completely filled \(d^{10}\) subshell both in their ground state and in their common oxidation states?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
According to IUPAC, transition metals are defined as metals that possess an incomplete \(d\) subshell either in their neutral atom or in any of their common ions.

Step 2: Evaluation
The elements of Group 12—zinc (\(\mathrm{Zn}\)), cadmium (\(\mathrm{Cd}\)), mercury (\(\mathrm{Hg}\)), and copernicium (\(\mathrm{Cn}\))—have the outer electronic configuration \((n-1)d^{10}ns^2\). In their common \(+2\) oxidation state, they lose the two \(ns\) electrons and retain a completely filled \((n-1)d^{10}\) configuration.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Because they lack an incompletely filled \(d\) subshell in both the ground state and common oxidised states, Group 12 elements (\(\mathrm{Zn}\), \(\mathrm{Cd}\), \(\mathrm{Hg}\), \(\mathrm{Cn}\)) are not regarded as transition metals.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT8_Q02 - Why scandium is a transition element

questiontext.text: Scandium (\(Z = 21\)) is regarded as a transition element whereas zinc (\(Z = 30\)) is not. What is the correct reason for this classification?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A \(d\)-block element is classified as a transition element if it has an incompletely filled \(d\) orbital in its ground state or in any stable oxidation state.

Step 2: Evaluation
Scandium (\(Z = 21\)) has the ground state electronic configuration \([\mathrm{Ar}]3d^14s^2\), which contains an incompletely filled \(3d^1\) orbital. In contrast, zinc (\(Z = 30\)) has the ground state configuration \([\mathrm{Ar}]3d^{10}4s^2\) and forms only \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\) with configuration \([\mathrm{Ar}]3d^{10}\), so its \(3d\) subshell is completely filled in both states.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Scandium is a transition element because it has incompletely filled \(3d\) orbitals in its ground state, whereas zinc has completely filled \(3d^{10}\) orbitals in both its ground and oxidised states.

answer.text: Scandium has incompletely filled \(3d\) orbitals (\(3d^1\)) in its ground state, while zinc has completely filled \(3d^{10}\) orbitals in both ground and oxidised states.
Scandium exhibits variable oxidation states from \(+1\) to \(+3\), while zinc exhibits only \(+2\).
Scandium forms coloured \(\mathrm{Sc^{3+}}\) ions in aqueous solution, while \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\) is colourless.
Scandium has a smaller atomic radius than zinc.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT8_Q03 - Ground state electronic configurations of Cr and Cu

questiontext.text: What are the ground-state outer electronic configurations of chromium (\(Z = 24\)) and copper (\(Z = 29\)), respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The general outer electronic configuration of \(d\)-block elements is \((n-1)d^{1-10}ns^{1-2}\). However, exceptions occur because the energy difference between \((n-1)d\) and \(ns\) orbitals is very small, and half-filled (\(d^5\)) and completely filled (\(d^{10}\)) sets of orbitals possess extra stability.

Step 2: Evaluation
For chromium (\(Z = 24\)), instead of \(3d^44s^2\), one \(4s\) electron shifts to the \(3d\) subshell to give the half-filled \(3d^54s^1\) configuration. For copper (\(Z = 29\)), instead of \(3d^94s^2\), one \(4s\) electron shifts to give the completely filled \(3d^{10}4s^1\) configuration.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The ground-state outer electronic configurations of \(\mathrm{Cr}\) and \(\mathrm{Cu}\) are \(3d^54s^1\) and \(3d^{10}4s^1\), respectively.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT8_Q04 - Ground state configurations of Pd and Pt

questiontext.text: Which of the following correctly represents the ground-state outer electronic configurations of palladium (\(Z = 46\)) and platinum (\(Z = 78\)), respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In the \(4d\) and \(5d\) transition series, relativistic effects and small energy gaps between \((n-1)d\) and \(ns\) orbitals lead to notable exceptions to the \((n-1)d^{1-10}ns^2\) pattern.

Step 2: Evaluation
Palladium (\(Z = 46\)) in the \(4d\) series has a completely filled \(4d\) subshell with zero electrons in the \(5s\) orbital, giving the outer configuration \(4d^{10}5s^0\). Platinum (\(Z = 78\)) in the \(5d\) series has one electron in the \(6s\) orbital and nine in the \(5d\) subshell, giving \(5d^96s^1\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The ground-state outer electronic configurations of palladium and platinum are \(4d^{10}5s^0\) and \(5d^96s^1\), respectively.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT8_Q05 - Why silver is a transition element

questiontext.text: Silver (\(Z = 47\)) has a completely filled \(4d^{10}\) subshell in its ground state (\([\mathrm{Kr}]4d^{10}5s^1\)). On what basis is silver still classified as a transition element?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
According to IUPAC, an element is a transition metal if it has an incomplete \(d\) subshell either in the neutral atom or in any of its ions.

Step 2: Evaluation
Although silver has a \(4d^{10}5s^1\) configuration in its ground state and \(4d^{10}\) in \(\mathrm{Ag^+}\), silver also exhibits a \(+2\) oxidation state (as in \(\mathrm{AgF_2}\)). In the \(\mathrm{Ag^{2+}}\) ion, the electronic configuration is \([\mathrm{Kr}]4d^9\), which has an incompletely filled \(4d\) subshell.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Silver is classified as a transition element because it exhibits a \(+2\) oxidation state in which it possesses an incompletely filled \(4d^9\) subshell.

answer.text: It has an incomplete \(5s\) orbital in its ground state.
It can exhibit a \(+2\) oxidation state where it has an incompletely filled \(4d^9\) orbital.
It belongs to Group 11 of the periodic table and has high electrical conductivity.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT8_Q06 - Matching transition metal ions with d configurations

questiontext.text:
Match the transition metal ions in Column I with their corresponding outer \(3d\) electronic configurations in Column II:

Column I (Ion)Column II (Configuration)
1. \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}\) (\(Z=24\))P. \(3d^5\)
2. \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) (\(Z=26\))Q. \(3d^3\)
3. \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\) (\(Z=25\))R. \(3d^7\)
4. \(\mathrm{Co^{2+}}\) (\(Z=27\))S. \(3d^6\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
When \(3d\)-block metals form cations, electrons are removed first from the outermost \(4s\) orbital and then from the \(3d\) orbitals.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Ion
1. \(\mathrm{Cr}\) (\(Z=24\)) is \([\mathrm{Ar}]3d^54s^1\); removing 3 electrons (one \(4s\) and two \(3d\)) gives \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}\) as \([\mathrm{Ar}]3d^3\).
2. \(\mathrm{Fe}\) (\(Z=26\)) is \([\mathrm{Ar}]3d^64s^2\); removing 2 electrons from \(4s\) gives \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) as \([\mathrm{Ar}]3d^6\).
3. \(\mathrm{Mn}\) (\(Z=25\)) is \([\mathrm{Ar}]3d^54s^2\); removing 2 electrons from \(4s\) gives \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\) as \([\mathrm{Ar}]3d^5\).
4. \(\mathrm{Co}\) (\(Z=27\)) is \([\mathrm{Ar}]3d^74s^2\); removing 2 electrons from \(4s\) gives \(\mathrm{Co^{2+}}\) as \([\mathrm{Ar}]3d^7\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct matching is \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}} \rightarrow 3d^3\), \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}} \rightarrow 3d^6\), \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}} \rightarrow 3d^5\), and \(\mathrm{Co^{2+}} \rightarrow 3d^7\), i.e., 1-Q, 2-S, 3-P, 4-R.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT8_Q07 - Statement question on d-orbital properties and horizontal similarities

questiontext.text:
Read the following two statements carefully and choose the correct evaluation:

Statement I: The \(d\) orbitals of transition elements protrude to the periphery of an atom more than \(s\) and \(p\) orbitals, making them more influenced by their surroundings.

Statement II: In contrast to non-transition elements, transition elements show greater similarities in properties along a horizontal row than within a vertical group.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The spatial extension of \((n-1)d\) orbitals and the progressive filling of inner \(d\) subshells govern the chemical and physical similarities among transition elements.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Statement
The first statement is correct: \(d\) orbitals protrude further toward the periphery of the atom than \(s\) and \(p\) orbitals, so they are more strongly influenced by surrounding ligands and atoms. The second statement is also correct: because electrons are added to the inner \((n-1)d\) subshell while the outer \(ns\) shell remains nearly unchanged across a period, transition elements exhibit greater horizontal similarities across a row than non-transition elements do.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Both statements are factually correct.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct, but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect, but Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT8_Q08 - Assertion reason on ionisation of ns vs d electrons

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): When \(3d\)-block elements form cations, \(4s\) electrons are lost before \(3d\) electrons.

Reason (R): In a neutral \(3d\)-series atom, the \(3d\) orbitals are always higher in energy than the \(4s\) orbital, and removing an electron leaves the \(3d\) orbitals unaffected.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Upon ionisation of \(d\)-block atoms, the outermost \(ns\) electrons are lost before the inner \((n-1)d\) electrons because the removal of an electron increases effective nuclear charge and lowers the energy of the \((n-1)d\) orbitals relative to \(ns\).

Step 2: Evaluation
The assertion is correct: \(4s\) electrons are indeed lost before \(3d\) electrons when \(3d\)-block elements form ions. However, the reason is false: in neutral atoms (and especially once electrons are removed), the relative energies of \(4s\) and \(3d\) orbitals change upon ionisation—\(3d\) orbitals become lower in energy than \(4s\) in the ions, rather than remaining unaffected or always higher.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The assertion is true, while the reason is false.

answer.text: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT8_Q09 - Lowest enthalpy of atomisation in 3d series

questiontext.text: In the \(3d\) series from \(\mathrm{Sc}\) (\(Z = 21\)) to \(\mathrm{Zn}\) (\(Z = 30\)), zinc has the lowest enthalpy of atomisation (\(126\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\)). Why?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The high enthalpy of atomisation of transition metals arises from strong interatomic metallic bonding involving both \(ns\) and unpaired \((n-1)d\) electrons.

Step 2: Evaluation
Zinc has a completely filled \(3d^{10}4s^2\) configuration with zero unpaired \(d\) electrons. Consequently, no electrons from the \(3d\) orbitals are involved in metallic bonding in zinc, resulting in weak interatomic interactions and the lowest enthalpy of atomisation in the \(3d\) series.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
No \(3d\) electrons are involved in the formation of metallic bonds in zinc.

answer.text: Zinc has the smallest atomic radius in the \(3d\) series.
Zinc has the lowest first ionisation enthalpy in the \(3d\) series.
No electrons from the \(3d\) orbitals are involved in metallic bonding in zinc.
Zinc forms a body-centred cubic lattice with weak \(4s\) overlap.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT8_Q10 - High enthalpies of atomisation of transition metals

questiontext.text: Transition elements generally exhibit very high enthalpies of atomisation primarily because:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Enthalpy of atomisation is the energy required to break the metallic lattice into individual gaseous atoms, which directly reflects the strength of interatomic metallic bonding.

Step 2: Evaluation
Transition metal atoms contain a large number of unpaired \((n-1)d\) electrons in addition to \(ns\) electrons. These electrons participate in strong interatomic interactions and metallic bonding, leading to high enthalpies of atomisation.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
High enthalpies of atomisation result from the large number of unpaired electrons producing strong interatomic metallic bonding.

answer.text: they have very low densities and high volatility
they possess a large number of unpaired electrons leading to strong interatomic bonding
their \(ns\) electrons are completely shielded by \(4f\) orbitals

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT8_Q11 - Melting point maxima and anomalies in transition series

questiontext.text: In the \(3d\) and \(4d\) transition series, the melting points rise to a maximum at the \(d^5\) configuration (\(\mathrm{Cr}\) and \(\mathrm{Mo}\)), except for anomalous low values observed for which pair of elements?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Melting points of transition metals generally increase with the number of unpaired \(d\) electrons, peaking near the middle of each series at \(d^5\).

Step 2: Evaluation
In the \(3d\) series, manganese (\(\mathrm{Mn}\)) shows an anomalously low melting point despite having a \(3d^54s^2\) configuration. Similarly, in the \(4d\) series, technetium (\(\mathrm{Tc}\)) exhibits an anomalously low melting point. This occurs because their stable half-filled \(d^5\) subshells hold electrons more tightly, reducing their participation in metallic bonding.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The anomalous low melting point values are observed for \(\mathrm{Mn}\) and \(\mathrm{Tc}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT8_Q12 - Metal-metal bonding in heavier transition series

questiontext.text: Why do compounds of the second (\(4d\)) and third (\(5d\)) transition series exhibit much more frequent metal–metal bonding than those of the first (\(3d\)) series?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The tendency to form metal–metal bonds correlates with the strength of interatomic interaction, which is reflected in the enthalpy of atomisation.

Step 2: Evaluation
Metals of the \(4d\) and \(5d\) series have significantly greater enthalpies of atomisation than the corresponding elements of the \(3d\) series. Stronger \(d\)–\(d\) orbital overlap in the heavier elements accounts for both their higher enthalpies of atomisation and the much more frequent occurrence of metal–metal bonding in their compounds.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The heavier \(4d\) and \(5d\) transition metals have greater enthalpies of atomisation than the corresponding \(3d\) metals.

answer.text: They have lower melting points and higher volatility than \(3d\) metals.
They have smaller atomic radii than \(3d\) metals.
They have greater enthalpies of atomisation than the corresponding \(3d\) elements.
They exhibit only \(+2\) oxidation state in their compounds.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT8_Q13 - Similarity of Zr and Hf radii due to lanthanoid contraction

questiontext.text: Zirconium (\(\mathrm{Zr}\), atomic radius \(160\,\mathrm{pm}\)) and hafnium (\(\mathrm{Hf}\), atomic radius \(159\,\mathrm{pm}\)) have nearly identical atomic radii and very similar physical and chemical properties. This is a direct consequence of:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Normally, atomic radii increase down a group due to the addition of a new principal electron shell. However, before the \(5d\) series begins (after \(\mathrm{La}\)), the fourteen \(4f\) orbitals are filled.

Step 2: Evaluation
Because \(4f\) electrons provide very poor shielding from the increasing nuclear charge, the size of the atoms decreases steadily across the lanthanoid series (lanthanoid contraction). This contraction essentially compensates for the expected increase in atomic size from the \(4d\) to the \(5d\) series, making \(\mathrm{Zr}\) (\(160\,\mathrm{pm}\)) and \(\mathrm{Hf}\) (\(159\,\mathrm{pm}\)) virtually identical in size.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The nearly identical radii of \(\mathrm{Zr}\) and \(\mathrm{Hf}\) result from lanthanoid contraction.

the inert pair effect in Group 4 elements
actinoid contraction due to the filling of \(5f\) orbitals
complete shielding of outer electrons by \(3d\) orbitals

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT8_Q14 - Density trend from titanium to copper

questiontext.text: From titanium (\(Z = 22\)) to copper (\(Z = 29\)) in the first transition series, there is a significant general increase in density. What accounts for this trend?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Density is defined as mass per unit volume (\(\rho = m/V\)). In metallic solids, volume per atom is proportional to the cube of the metallic radius.

Step 2: Evaluation
Moving from \(\mathrm{Ti}\) (\(Z = 22\)) to \(\mathrm{Cu}\) (\(Z = 29\)), the atomic mass increases steadily while the metallic radius generally decreases (from \(147\,\mathrm{pm}\) in \(\mathrm{Ti}\) to \(128\,\mathrm{pm}\) in \(\mathrm{Cu}\)). Both factors—higher mass and smaller atomic volume—combine to cause a significant increase in density (from \(4.1\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}\) to \(8.9\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The general increase in density from \(\mathrm{Ti}\) to \(\mathrm{Cu}\) is caused by a decrease in metallic radius coupled with an increase in atomic mass.

Decrease in metallic radius coupled with increase in atomic mass
Decrease in nuclear charge coupled with increase in \(4s\) shielding
Transition from ccp structure to open bcc structure

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT8_Q15 - Lattice structures of 3d transition metals

questiontext.text: At normal temperatures, which of the following \(3d\) transition metals adopts a body-centred cubic (bcc) lattice structure?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Most transition metals adopt one or more typical close-packed or body-centred metallic structures at normal temperatures: hcp, ccp, or bcc.

Step 2: Evaluation
In the \(3d\) series, \(\mathrm{Sc}\) and \(\mathrm{Ti}\) adopt hcp (with bcc at higher temperatures); \(\mathrm{V}\), \(\mathrm{Cr}\), and \(\mathrm{Fe}\) adopt bcc structures; \(\mathrm{Co}\), \(\mathrm{Ni}\), and \(\mathrm{Cu}\) adopt ccp structures; and \(\mathrm{Mn}\) and \(\mathrm{Zn}\) have atypical/complex metallic structures.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Among the given metals, chromium (\(\mathrm{Cr}\)) adopts a bcc lattice structure at normal temperatures.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT8_Q16 - Graph based melting point trend in 3d series

questiontext.text:

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT8_Q17 - Assertion reason on shielding of 4f vs d electrons

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): The atomic radii of the third (\(5d\)) transition series elements are virtually the same as those of the corresponding members of the second (\(4d\)) transition series.

Reason (R): The shielding of one \(4f\) electron by another is less effective than that of one \(d\) electron by another, resulting in lanthanoid contraction before the \(5d\) series begins.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Shielding efficiency follows the order \(s > p > d > f\). Imperfect shielding in the \(4f\) subshell causes a steady contraction in atomic size across the lanthanoid series.

Step 2: Evaluation
The assertion is true: \(5d\) transition metals have almost the same atomic radii as their \(4d\) congeners (for example, \(\mathrm{Zr}\) and \(\mathrm{Hf}\)). The reason is also true and directly explains the assertion: because \(4f\) orbitals are filled before \(5d\) orbitals and \(4f\) electrons shield each other even less effectively than \(d\) electrons, the resulting lanthanoid contraction cancels out the expected shell-size increase from \(4d\) to \(5d\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Both the assertion and the reason are true, and the reason is the correct explanation of the assertion.

answer.text: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT8_Q18 - Variation of first ionisation enthalpy across 3d series

questiontext.text: Why does the first ionisation enthalpy increase only slightly across the \(3d\) transition series compared to a period of non-transition elements?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Ionisation enthalpy depends on effective nuclear charge and atomic radius.

Step 2: Evaluation
As nuclear charge increases from \(\mathrm{Sc}\) to \(\mathrm{Zn}\), the added electrons enter the inner \(3d\) subshell. These inner \(3d\) electrons shield the outer \(4s\) electrons from the increasing nuclear charge more effectively than outer-shell electrons shield one another. Consequently, atomic radii decrease less rapidly and first ionisation enthalpies increase only slightly along the \(3d\) series.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The added \(3d\) electrons shield the outer \(4s\) electrons effectively, causing atomic radii to decrease less rapidly.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT8_Q19 - Unusually high second ionisation enthalpy of Cr and Cu

questiontext.text: Which pair of elements in the \(3d\) series exhibits unusually high second ionisation enthalpies (\(\Delta_i H^\circ_{\mathrm{II}}\)) due to the extra stability of \(d^5\) and \(d^{10}\) configurations of their \(\mathrm{M^+}\) ions?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Second ionisation enthalpy is the energy required to remove an electron from a gaseous \(\mathrm{M^+}\) ion to form \(\mathrm{M^{2+}}\). Removing an electron from a stable half-filled (\(d^5\)) or completely filled (\(d^{10}\)) configuration requires unusually high energy.

Step 2: Evaluation
After losing one \(4s\) electron, \(\mathrm{Cr^+}\) has the \(3d^5\) configuration and \(\mathrm{Cu^+}\) has the \(3d^{10}\) configuration. Disrupting these extra-stable configurations leads to unusually high second ionisation enthalpies for \(\mathrm{Cr}\) (\(1592\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\)) and \(\mathrm{Cu}\) (\(1958\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The pair of elements showing unusually high second ionisation enthalpies is \(\mathrm{Cr}\) and \(\mathrm{Cu}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT8_Q20 - Third ionisation enthalpy of Fe vs Mn

questiontext.text: Why is the third ionisation enthalpy of iron (\(\mathrm{Fe}\)) lower than that of manganese (\(\mathrm{Mn}\))?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Third ionisation enthalpy corresponds to the process \(\mathrm{M^{2+}}(g) \rightarrow \mathrm{M^{3+}}(g) + e^-\). The stability of a half-filled \(3d^5\) subshell strongly influences the energy required.

Step 2: Evaluation
\(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\) has the extra-stable half-filled \(3d^5\) configuration, so removing a third electron to form \(3d^4\) (\(\mathrm{Mn^{3+}}\)) results in a large loss of exchange energy and requires very high energy (\(3260\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\)). In contrast, \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) has a \(3d^6\) configuration; removing a third electron yields the stable half-filled \(3d^5\) configuration (\(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\)) with no loss of exchange energy, making the third ionisation enthalpy of \(\mathrm{Fe}\) (\(2962\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\)) lower.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) (\(3d^6\)) attains the stable \(3d^5\) configuration upon losing an electron, whereas \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\) (\(3d^5\)) loses its stable half-filled configuration.

answer.text: \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) (\(3d^6\)) loses an electron to achieve the stable \(3d^5\) configuration, whereas \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\) (\(3d^5\)) must lose an electron from a stable half-filled \(3d^5\) configuration.
\(\mathrm{Fe}\) has a smaller nuclear charge than \(\mathrm{Mn}\).
\(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\) still contains a \(4s^1\) electron that is tightly held.
\(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\) has a \(3d^4\) configuration which has higher exchange energy than \(\mathrm{Mn^{3+}}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT8_Q21 - Difficulty in obtaining oxidation state above +2 for Cu, Ni, Zn

questiontext.text: Why is it very difficult to obtain an oxidation state greater than \(+2\) for copper, nickel, and zinc?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Forming an \(\mathrm{M^{3+}}\) ion from \(\mathrm{M^{2+}}\) requires supplying the third ionisation enthalpy (\(\Delta_i H^\circ_{\mathrm{III}}\)).

Step 2: Evaluation
At the end of the \(3d\) series, the effective nuclear charge is high and the \(3d\) orbitals are contracted. Consequently, the third ionisation enthalpies of nickel (\(3402\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\)), copper (\(3556\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\)), and zinc (\(3837\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\)) are extremely high—especially for \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\) (\(3d^{10}\)). This makes oxidation beyond \(+2\) energetically unfavourable.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The high values of their third ionisation enthalpies make it difficult to obtain oxidation states greater than \(+2\) for \(\mathrm{Ni}\), \(\mathrm{Cu}\), and \(\mathrm{Zn}\).

answer.text: They have very low enthalpies of atomisation.
Their third ionisation enthalpies are very high.
Their hydration enthalpies for \(\mathrm{M^{3+}}\) ions are endothermic.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT8_Q22 - Exchange energy and second ionisation enthalpy of Mn vs Cr

questiontext.text:
Read the following statements regarding exchange energy and ionisation enthalpies in the \(3d\) series:

Statement I: Exchange energy is approximately proportional to the total number of possible pairs of parallel spins in degenerate orbitals, and there is no loss of exchange energy at the \(d^6\) configuration.

Statement II: The second ionisation enthalpy of \(\mathrm{Mn}\) is lower than that of \(\mathrm{Cr}\).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Ionisation enthalpy is governed by nuclear attraction, inter-electronic repulsion, and exchange energy. Exchange energy stabilises states with maximum parallel spins in degenerate orbitals.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Statement
At the \(d^6\) configuration, the sixth electron pairs up, so removing that sixth electron to form \(d^5\) causes no loss of exchange energy. Thus, the first statement is correct. For the second ionisation enthalpy, \(\mathrm{Mn^+}\) has the \(3d^54s^1\) configuration (losing the \(4s^1\) electron gives \(3d^5\)), whereas \(\mathrm{Cr^+}\) has the \(3d^5\) configuration (losing an electron disrupts the stable \(3d^5\) state). name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT8_Q23 - Element exhibiting largest number of oxidation states in 3d series

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Manganese (\(\mathrm{Mn}\)) exhibits the largest number of oxidation states in the \(3d\) series.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT8_Q24 - Transition element without variable oxidation states

questiontext.text: Which of the following \(3d\) transition elements does NOT exhibit variable oxidation states?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Transition elements typically display variable oxidation states due to the participation of \((n-1)d\) and \(ns\) electrons of comparable energy.

Step 2: Evaluation

Scandium (\(\mathrm{Sc}\)) does not exhibit variable oxidation states.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT8_Q25 - Variability of oxidation states in d-block vs p-block

questiontext.text: How does the variability in oxidation states of transition metals differ from that of non-transition (\(p\)-block) elements?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Oxidation state variability depends on the orbitals involved in bonding.

Step 2: Evaluation
In transition elements, incomplete filling of \(d\) orbitals allows electrons to be lost or shared one by one, so consecutive oxidation states differ by unity (for example, \(\mathrm{V^{II}}, \mathrm{V^{III}}, \mathrm{V^{IV}}, \mathrm{V^{V}}\)). In \(p\)-block elements, oxidation states normally differ by a unit of two (for example, \(+2\) and \(+4\) or \(+3\) and \(+5\)) due to the inert pair effect.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Oxidation states of transition elements differ from each other by unity, whereas those of non-transition elements normally differ by two.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT8_Q27 - Zero oxidation state in metal carbonyls

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT8_Q28 - Oxometal anions with oxidation state equal to group number

questiontext.text: In which of the following oxometal species does the transition metal exhibit an oxidation state equal to its group number?

generalfeedback.text:

The maximum oxidation state of early \(3d\) transition metals up to manganese corresponds to the sum of their \(4s\) and \(3d\) electrons, which equals their group number.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{VO_2^+}\), \(\mathrm{CrO_4^{2-}}\), and \(\mathrm{MnO_4^-}\) all have metal oxidation states equal to their group numbers.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT8_Q29 - Positive standard electrode potential of copper

questiontext.text: The standard electrode potential \(E^\circ(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}/Cu})\) is positive (\(+0.34\,\mathrm{V}\)), unlike other first-row transition metals. What is the reason for this positive value?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The standard electrode potential \(E^\circ(\mathrm{M^{2+}/M})\) depends on the sum of enthalpy of atomisation (\(\Delta_a H^\circ\)), first and second ionisation enthalpies (\(\Delta_i H_1 + \Delta_i H_2\)), and hydration enthalpy (\(\Delta_{\mathrm{hyd}}H^\circ\)).

Step 2: Evaluation
To convert \(\mathrm{Cu(s)}\) to \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}(aq)}\), a large amount of energy is required due to copper's high enthalpy of atomisation and high first and second ionisation enthalpies. This high energy input is not compensated by the negative hydration enthalpy of \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\). As a result, \(E^\circ(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}/Cu})\) is positive (\(+0.34\,\mathrm{V}\)), and copper cannot liberate \(\mathrm{H_2}\) from dilute non-oxidising acids.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The high energy required to transform \(\mathrm{Cu(s)}\) to \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}(aq)}\) is not balanced by its hydration enthalpy.

answer.text: Copper has a very low enthalpy of atomisation and very high hydration enthalpy.
Copper has a completely filled \(3d^{10}\) configuration in \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT8_Q30 - Why Cr2+ is reducing and Mn3+ is oxidising

questiontext.text: Both \(\mathrm{Cr^{2+}}\) and \(\mathrm{Mn^{3+}}\) have the \(3d^4\) electronic configuration, yet \(\mathrm{Cr^{2+}}\) is strongly reducing while \(\mathrm{Mn^{3+}}\) is strongly oxidising. Why?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A reducing agent undergoes oxidation (loses an electron), while an oxidising agent undergoes reduction (gains an electron). The driving force is the stability of the resulting \(d\)-electron configuration.

Step 2: Evaluation
When \(\mathrm{Cr^{2+}}\) (\(d^4\)) is oxidised to \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}\), its configuration changes from \(d^4\) to \(d^3\), which has a stable half-filled \(t_{2g}\) level in octahedral aqueous coordination. Conversely, when \(\mathrm{Mn^{3+}}\) (\(d^4\)) is reduced to \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\), its configuration changes from \(d^4\) to \(d^5\), achieving the extra-stable half-filled \(3d^5\) configuration.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{Cr^{2+}}\) is reducing because it forms stable \(d^3\) (\(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}\)), and \(\mathrm{Mn^{3+}}\) is oxidising because it forms stable \(d^5\) (\(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\)).

answer.text: \(\mathrm{Cr^{2+}}\) changes from \(d^4\) to \(d^5\), while \(\mathrm{Mn^{3+}}\) changes from \(d^4\) to \(d^3\).
\(\mathrm{Cr^{2+}}\) changes from \(d^4\) to \(d^3\) (half-filled \(t_{2g}\) level), while \(\mathrm{Mn^{3+}}\) changes from \(d^4\) to \(d^5\) (half-filled \(d\) subshell).
\(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}\) has a higher third ionisation enthalpy than \(\mathrm{Mn^{3+}}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT8_Q31 - More negative E0 values for Mn, Ni, and Zn

questiontext.text: Across the \(3d\) series, \(E^\circ(\mathrm{M^{2+}/M})\) generally becomes less negative, but \(\mathrm{Mn}\), \(\mathrm{Ni}\), and \(\mathrm{Zn}\) show more negative values than expected from the trend. What is the reason specifically for nickel (\(\mathrm{Ni}\))?

More negative \(E^\circ(\mathrm{M^{2+}/M})\) values indicate greater thermodynamic stability of \(\mathrm{M^{2+}}(aq)\) relative to \(\mathrm{M}(s)\).

Step 2: Evaluation
For \(\mathrm{Mn}\) and \(\mathrm{Zn}\), the more negative \(E^\circ\) values are linked to the stability of the half-filled \(3d^5\) configuration in \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\) and the completely filled \(3d^{10}\) configuration in \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\). For nickel, \(\mathrm{Ni^{2+}}\) (\(3d^8\)) does not have a \(d^5\) or \(d^{10}\) configuration; instead, its more negative \(E^\circ\) (\(-0.25\,\mathrm{V}\)) is related to its highest negative enthalpy of hydration (\(-2121\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The more negative \(E^\circ\) value for nickel is due to the highest negative enthalpy of hydration of \(\mathrm{Ni^{2+}}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT8_Q32 - Instability and disproportionation of Cu+ in aqueous solution

questiontext.text: Many copper(I) compounds are unstable in aqueous solution and undergo disproportionation according to \(2\mathrm{Cu^+}(aq) \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu^{2+}}(aq) + \mathrm{Cu}(s)\). Why is \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}(aq)\) more stable than \(\mathrm{Cu^+}(aq)\)?

generalfeedback.text:

Stability of an ion in aqueous solution depends on the balance between ionisation enthalpy required to form the ion and the hydration enthalpy released when it is hydrated.

Although forming \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) from \(\mathrm{Cu^+}\) requires a high second ionisation enthalpy, \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}(aq)\) has a much higher charge density and therefore a much more negative enthalpy of hydration (\(\Delta_{\mathrm{hyd}}H^\circ\)) than \(\mathrm{Cu^+}(aq)\). This large hydration enthalpy more than compensates for the second ionisation enthalpy of copper.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The much more negative \(\Delta_{\mathrm{hyd}}H^\circ\) of \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}(aq)\) compared to \(\mathrm{Cu^+}(aq)\) more than compensates for the second ionisation enthalpy of \(\mathrm{Cu}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT8_Q33 - Reaction of Cu2+ with iodide ion

questiontext.text: All copper(II) halides are known except copper(II) iodide. What happens when \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) ions react with \(\mathrm{I^-}\) ions in aqueous solution?

Step 1: Conceptual Principle

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT8_Q34 - Why oxygen stabilises higher oxidation states than fluorine

questiontext.text: The highest fluoride of manganese is \(\mathrm{MnF_4}\) (\(+4\)), whereas the highest oxide is \(\mathrm{Mn_2O_7}\) (\(+7\)). Why does oxygen stabilise higher oxidation states better than fluorine?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Both fluorine and oxygen are small and highly electronegative, enabling them to oxidise metals to high oxidation states. However, their bonding capabilities with transition metals differ.

Step 2: Evaluation
Fluorine can only form single bonds with a metal atom, limiting the coordination and oxidation number (e.g., \(\mathrm{MnF_4}\)). Oxygen, on the other hand, has the ability to form multiple bonds (\(p\pi\text{–}d\pi\) double bonds) to transition metals, allowing it to stabilise higher oxidation states such as \(+7\) in \(\mathrm{Mn_2O_7}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The ability of oxygen to form multiple bonds to metals explains its superiority over fluorine in stabilising high oxidation states.

Oxygen has the ability to form multiple bonds to metals.
\(\mathrm{Mn_2O_7}\) is an ionic solid with higher lattice energy than \(\mathrm{MnF_4}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT8_Q36 - Disproportionation of manganate(VI) in acidic solution

questiontext.text: In acidic solution, the manganate(VI) ion (\(\mathrm{MnO_4^{2-}}\)) undergoes disproportionation. What are the manganese-containing products formed?

generalfeedback.text:

Disproportionation occurs when an intermediate oxidation state is less stable relative to one higher and one lower oxidation state, so it simultaneously oxidises and reduces itself.

The manganese-containing products are \(\mathrm{MnO_4^-}\) and \(\mathrm{MnO_2}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT8_Q38 - Spin-only magnetic moment of divalent ion Z=25

questiontext.text: Calculate the spin-only magnetic moment of a divalent ion in aqueous solution if its atomic number is \(25\).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Atomic number \(Z = 25\) (Manganese, \(\mathrm{Mn}\)), divalent ion \(\mathrm{M^{2+}}\) in aqueous solution.

Step 2: Relevant Formulae
The spin-only magnetic moment is \(\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}\,\mathrm{BM}\), where \(n\) is the number of unpaired electrons.

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
1. Neutral \(\mathrm{Mn}\) (\(Z = 25\)) has the electronic configuration \([\mathrm{Ar}]3d^54s^2\).
2. Removing two \(4s\) electrons gives \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\) with configuration \([\mathrm{Ar}]3d^5\).
3. In \(3d^5\), all five \(3d\) orbitals are singly occupied, so \(n = 5\).
4. Substituting \(n = 5\):
\(\mu = \sqrt{5(5+2)} = \sqrt{35} \approx 5.92\,\mathrm{BM}\).

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
Five unpaired electrons correspond to \(\approx 5.92\,\mathrm{BM}\). The spin-only magnetic moment is \(5.92\,\mathrm{BM}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT8_Q39 - Spin-only magnetic moment of divalent ion Z=27

questiontext.text: What is the calculated spin-only magnetic moment of an \(\mathrm{M^{2+}}(aq)\) ion with atomic number \(Z = 27\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions

Step 2: Relevant Formulae
Spin-only magnetic moment: \(\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}\,\mathrm{BM}\).

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
1. Neutral \(\mathrm{Co}\) (\(Z = 27\)) has configuration \([\mathrm{Ar}]3d^74s^2\).
2. Losing the two \(4s\) electrons gives \(\mathrm{Co^{2+}}\) with configuration \([\mathrm{Ar}]3d^7\).
3. Filling five \(3d\) orbitals according to Hund's rule gives two paired orbitals and three singly occupied orbitals, so \(n = 3\) unpaired electrons.
4. Substituting \(n = 3\):
\(\mu = \sqrt{3(3+2)} = \sqrt{15} \approx 3.87\,\mathrm{BM}\).

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
For \(n = 3\), \(\mu\) lies between \(3\) and \(4\,\mathrm{BM}\), specifically \(3.87\,\mathrm{BM}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT8_Q42 - Why transition metals form complex compounds

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT8_Q43 - Catalytic mechanism of Fe3+ in iodide-persulphate reaction

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT8_Q48 - Effect of increasing pH on potassium dichromate solution

Increasing the \(\mathrm{pH}\) converts orange \(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}}\) into yellow \(\mathrm{CrO_4^{2-}}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT8_Q49 - Stoichiometry of acidified dichromate oxidising Fe2+

questiontext.text: How many moles of \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) ions are oxidised to \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\) by \(1\,\mathrm{mol}\) of \(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}}\) in acidic medium?

\(1\,\mathrm{mol}\) of \(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}}\) reacts with \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) in acidic medium.

\(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}} + 14\mathrm{H^+} + 6e^- \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Cr^{3+}} + 7\mathrm{H_2O}\).

\(1\,\mathrm{mol}\) of \(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}}\) oxidises \(6\,\mathrm{mol}\) of \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT8_Q50 - Thermal decomposition and magnetic nature of KMnO4

In the green manganate ion (\(\mathrm{MnO_4^{2-}}\)), manganese is in the \(+6\) state (\(3d^1\)) and possesses one unpaired electron, which makes \(\mathrm{MnO_4^{2-}}\) paramagnetic.

The products are \(\mathrm{K_2MnO_4}\), \(\mathrm{MnO_2}\), and \(\mathrm{O_2}\), and \(\mathrm{MnO_4^{2-}}\) is paramagnetic due to one unpaired electron.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT8_Q51 - Oxidation of iodide by permanganate in neutral/alkaline medium

questiontext.text: In neutral or faintly alkaline solution, potassium permanganate oxidises iodide ion (\(\mathrm{I^-}\)) and thiosulphate ion (\(\mathrm{S_2O_3^{2-}}\)) to which species, respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In neutral or faintly alkaline medium, \(\mathrm{MnO_4^-}\) is reduced to \(\mathrm{MnO_2}\), and the oxidation products of reducing agents differ from those in strongly acidic medium.

Step 2: Evaluation of Reactions
1. With iodide ion in neutral or faintly alkaline solution, \(\mathrm{I^-}\) is oxidised to iodate (\(\mathrm{IO_3^-}\)) rather than \(\mathrm{I_2}\):
\(2\mathrm{MnO_4^-} + \mathrm{H_2O} + \mathrm{I^-} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{MnO_2} + 2\mathrm{OH^-} + \mathrm{IO_3^-}\).

Iodide is oxidised to \(\mathrm{IO_3^-}\) and thiosulphate is oxidised to \(\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT8_Q52 - Why HCl is avoided in permanganate titrations

questiontext.text: Why are potassium permanganate (\(\mathrm{KMnO_4}\)) titrations unsatisfactory in the presence of hydrochloric acid (\(\mathrm{HCl}\))?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
For an acid to be suitable in redox titrations with \(\mathrm{KMnO_4}\), it must only supply \(\mathrm{H^+}\) ions without reacting with the titrant (\(\mathrm{MnO_4^-}\)).

Step 2: Evaluation
Hydrochloric acid is unsatisfactory because \(\mathrm{MnO_4^-}\) is a strong enough oxidising agent to oxidise \(\mathrm{Cl^-}\) ions from \(\mathrm{HCl}\) into chlorine gas (\(\mathrm{Cl_2}\)). This consumes extra \(\mathrm{KMnO_4}\) and causes an error in the titration.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Permanganate titrations in the presence of \(\mathrm{HCl}\) are unsatisfactory because \(\mathrm{HCl}\) is oxidised to \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\).

\(\mathrm{HCl}\) is too weak an acid to maintain \([\mathrm{H^+}] = 1\,\mathrm{M}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT8_Q53 - Stoichiometry of acidified permanganate oxidising oxalate

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT8_Q54 - Predominant oxidation state and configuration of lanthanoids

questiontext.text: What is the most common and stable oxidation state of all lanthanoids (\(\mathrm{Ln}\)), and what is the general outer electronic configuration of their tripositive ions?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Lanthanoid atoms have a common \(6s^2\) outer shell with variable occupancy of the \(4f\) level (and \(5d^1\) in \(\mathrm{La}\), \(\mathrm{Ce}\), \(\mathrm{Gd}\), \(\mathrm{Lu}\)).

Step 2: Evaluation
Upon losing three electrons (two \(6s\) and one \(5d\) or \(4f\)), all lanthanoids form tripositive \(\mathrm{Ln^{3+}}\) ions, which represent their predominant and most stable oxidation state (\(+3\)). All \(\mathrm{Ln^{3+}}\) ions have the general electronic configuration \([\mathrm{Xe}]4f^n\) (where \(n = 1\) to \(14\) across \(\mathrm{Ce}\) to \(\mathrm{Lu}\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The most stable oxidation state is \(+3\) with the general configuration \([\mathrm{Xe}]4f^n\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT8_Q55 - Lanthanoids exhibiting +4 and +2 oxidation states

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements about the \(+2\) and \(+4\) oxidation states of lanthanoids is correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Although \(+3\) is the principal oxidation state of lanthanoids, \(+2\) and \(+4\) ions occur when they achieve extra-stable empty (\(f^0\)), half-filled (\(f^7\)), or completely filled (\(f^{14}\)) \(4f\) subshells. However, they tend to revert to the common \(+3\) state.

Step 2: Evaluation
1. \(\mathrm{Ce^{4+}}\) has the noble gas \(4f^0\) configuration, but it is a strong oxidant (\(E^\circ = +1.74\,\mathrm{V}\)) reverting to \(\mathrm{Ce^{3+}}\).
2. \(\mathrm{Eu^{2+}}\) has the half-filled \(4f^7\) configuration and \(\mathrm{Yb^{2+}}\) has the completely filled \(4f^{14}\) configuration; both act as strong reducing agents, changing to the common \(+3\) state.
3. \(\mathrm{Tb^{4+}}\) has a half-filled \(4f^7\) configuration and acts as an oxidant.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{Eu^{2+}}\) (\(4f^7\)) and \(\mathrm{Yb^{2+}}\) (\(4f^{14}\)) are strong reducing agents, whereas \(\mathrm{Ce^{4+}}\) (\(4f^0\)) is a strong oxidant.

\(\mathrm{Eu^{2+}}\) is a strong oxidising agent because of its \(4f^7\) configuration.
\(\mathrm{Eu^{2+}}\) and \(\mathrm{Yb^{2+}}\) are strong reducing agents, whereas \(\mathrm{Ce^{4+}}\) is a strong oxidant.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT8_Q56 - Spin-only magnetic moment of Ce3+ ion

questiontext.text: Using the spin-only formula, what is the magnetic moment of the \(\mathrm{Ce^{3+}}\) ion (\(Z = 58\))?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Cerium (\(\mathrm{Ce}\)) has atomic number \(Z = 58\); we consider the \(\mathrm{Ce^{3+}}\) ion.

Step 2: Relevant Formulae
Spin-only magnetic moment: \(\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}\,\mathrm{BM}\).

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
1. The ground-state electronic configuration of \(\mathrm{Ce}\) (\(Z = 58\)) is \([\mathrm{Xe}]4f^15d^16s^2\).
2. Removing three electrons (two \(6s\) and one \(5d\)) gives \(\mathrm{Ce^{3+}}\) with configuration \([\mathrm{Xe}]4f^1\).
3. Thus, \(\mathrm{Ce^{3+}}\) has \(n = 1\) unpaired electron.
4. \(\mu = \sqrt{1(1+2)} = \sqrt{3} \approx 1.73\,\mathrm{BM}\).

Step 4: Final Answer
The spin-only magnetic moment of \(\mathrm{Ce^{3+}}\) is \(1.73\,\mathrm{BM}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT8_Q57 - Colour and diamagnetism of La3+ and Lu3+

questiontext.text: Which pair of trivalent lanthanoid/lanthanum ions is both colourless and diamagnetic in aqueous solution?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Both colour (due to \(f\text{–}f\) transitions) and paramagnetism in lanthanoid ions depend on the presence of unpaired \(4f\) electrons. Ions with \(4f^0\) or \(4f^{14}\) configurations have no unpaired \(4f\) electrons and cannot undergo \(f\text{–}f\) transitions.

Step 2: Evaluation
\(\mathrm{La^{3+}}\) (\(Z = 57\)) has the \(4f^0\) configuration, and \(\mathrm{Lu^{3+}}\) (\(Z = 71\)) has the \(4f^{14}\) configuration. Neither ion has unpaired electrons, so both are colourless and diamagnetic. All other \(\mathrm{Ln^{3+}}\) ions (such as \(\mathrm{Ce^{3+}}\), \(\mathrm{Gd^{3+}}\), \(\mathrm{Eu^{3+}}\)) contain \(4f^1\) to \(4f^{13}\) electrons and are paramagnetic.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{La^{3+}}\) and \(\mathrm{Lu^{3+}}\) are both colourless and diamagnetic.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT8_Q58 - Chemical reactions of lanthanoids with C, N, S, and H2O

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT8_Q59 - Why actinoid contraction is greater than lanthanoid contraction

questiontext.text: Why is the actinoid contraction greater from element to element than the lanthanoid contraction?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Both lanthanoid and actinoid contractions arise from the increase in nuclear charge across the series coupled with imperfect shielding by \(f\) electrons.

Step 2: Evaluation
The \(5f\) orbitals in actinoids are more spatially extended and provide even poorer shielding from the increasing nuclear charge from element to element than the \(4f\) orbitals in lanthanoids. Consequently, the effective nuclear charge increases more sharply across the actinoid series, causing a greater contraction in atomic and ionic sizes from element to element.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Actinoid contraction is greater because \(5f\) electrons provide poorer shielding than \(4f\) electrons.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT8_Q60 - Comparison of oxidation states of actinoids and lanthanoids

questiontext.text: Why do actinoids exhibit a much wider range of oxidation states than lanthanoids?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The range of oxidation states exhibited by a series of elements depends on the energy separation between their valence subshells.

Step 2: Evaluation
In lanthanoids, the \(4f\) orbitals are deeply buried and much lower in energy than \(5d\) and \(6s\), so primarily \(+3\) (and occasionally \(+2, +4\)) states are observed. In actinoids, the \(5f\), \(6d\), and \(7s\) levels have comparable energies, and the \(5f\) orbitals are not as deeply buried as \(4f\), allowing all three sets of electrons to participate in bonding and giving rise to oxidation states from \(+3\) up to \(+7\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The \(5f\), \(6d\), and \(7s\) energy levels in actinoids are of comparable energies.

Actinoids are non-radioactive and have higher ionisation enthalpies than lanthanoids.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT8_Q61 - Electronic configuration and oxidation states of actinoids

questiontext.text: Which of the following correctly gives the ground-state outer electronic configuration of curium (\(\mathrm{Cm}, Z = 96\)) and the maximum oxidation state exhibited by neptunium (\(\mathrm{Np}, Z = 93\))?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Irregularities in the electronic configurations of actinoids arise from the extra stability of \(5f^0\), \(5f^7\), and \(5f^{14}\) occupancies.
